scenario: AITA for threatening to stop supporting my wife financially? | I will start by saying I pay for about 70-80% of me and my wife’s cost of living expenses (necessities). She makes about 1/3 what I do so I like for her to be able to save and have extra money for things she wants, vice dump it all into cost of living. My wife has a friend called Yasmin. Yasmin is part of some group (it has a spanish name so I don’t know what it is) that says they empower women. My wife told me about this group one day, apparently you submit $1000 (somewhere or to someone??) and become a level 1 group member, gaining levels by recruiting more members. Once you reach level 5 or so of the community, you have about 30 people under you, and you graduate from the community and receive $30,000. All the while the group is supposed to support each other and help you attain your goals by giving you that cash infusion at the end. The whole process is supposed to take 2 months. As soon as she told me about this, the words MLM, scam, and other things came to mind. In my opinion, this is some type of MLM disguised in a veil of “empowerment of women.” Yasmin is 4 months in and still trying to recruit people because she has not seen her money yet. Somehow Yasmin has convinced my wife to join this cause. I tried explaining to her that some MLMs *do* actually work, but those stories are few and far between and only to the insider people who started the whole thing in the first place, never the grunts that join later. I told her that if she does this she will 1) never see her money again 2) become an embarrassment to herself as she begins to essentially ask all her friends and family for money to join the program so that she can get hers 3) waste a lot of time when this never works out. I think she has good intentions, at least as far as wanting to make more money and contribute, but she has somehow gotten tricked into thinking this get rich quick maneuver will work. When she told me she wanted to join I fought her on it and told her that I will stop helping her pay for things on this main basis: I am currently doing so because I like to help her with her basic needs/necessities so she can spend her money on things she wants. Because this $1000->$30,000 is not a 100% guarantee, she is essentially gambling her money that she will turn a profit. In this perspective, she has money beyond her basic wants and she even has enough to gamble with, therefore there is no reason for me to still be supporting her needs/necessities. I will admit that I feel like I am using money to strong arm her into making a decision for her. I would normally never do this to her but I just feel so strongly that she is about to get screwed over and I don’t want to see that happen to her, so I am almost threatening her to save her from herself. I did end the conversation with, I cannot make the decision for you, I can just tell you my thoughts on the matter and inform you of the actions I am going to take if you still decide to do through with this.

message.reasoning:
Okay, so I'm trying to figure out whether the action described is morally acceptable or not. The scenario is about a husband who is threatening to stop financially supporting his wife if she joins a certain group that he believes is a scam. Let me break this down step by step.

First, the husband is contributing about 70-80% of their living expenses, which is a significant amount. His wife makes about a third of what he does, so he's trying to help her save and have extra money for things she wants. That seems like a good intention on his part.

Now, the wife wants to join this group called something with a Spanish name, which the husband thinks is an MLM (Multi-Level Marketing) scheme. He's warning her that it's likely a scam, pointing out that most MLMs don't work out for the people who join later. He's concerned that she'll lose money, become an embarrassment by asking others for money, and waste time on something that won't succeed.

The husband's approach is to threaten to stop supporting her financially if she goes through with joining the group. He's using money as leverage to influence her decision, which he admits feels like strong-arming her. He says he's doing this because he doesn't want to see her get scammed and that he's trying to protect her.

On the surface, his intention is to protect his wife from financial loss and potential embarrassment. However, the method he's using—threatening to withdraw financial support—is concerning. It's manipulative because he's using his control over the finances to force her into making a decision he thinks is better for her.

I also need to consider the dynamics of their relationship. If the husband is the primary breadwinner, he might feel entitled to have more control over how the money is spent. But that doesn't necessarily make his actions morally acceptable. The wife has her own right to make decisions about her money and her life, even if the husband disagrees with them.

Another angle is the concept of consent. The husband is essentially forcing his wife to make a decision by threatening to withhold financial support. This undermines her autonomy and could damage their relationship trust.

Additionally, the husband's belief that the group is a scam is based on his own judgment. While his concerns are valid, he might not have all the information. The wife might have her reasons for wanting to join, and she deserves the chance to make her own choices, even if they don't align with his views.

In terms of morality, actions that involve manipulation or coercion to control another person's decisions are generally considered unethical. The husband's threat is a form of coercion, which is not morally acceptable, even if his intentions are to protect his wife.

Moreover, the husband's approach doesn't foster open communication or mutual respect. Instead of having a dialogue where both parties can express their perspectives and work towards a compromise, he's using a power play to enforce his will. This can lead to resentment and a breakdown in the relationship.

It's also worth considering the potential consequences of his action. If he follows through on his threat, it could leave the wife in a difficult financial situation, especially if she's not prepared to handle the expenses on her own. This could lead to further stress and conflict between them.

In conclusion, while the husband's intention to protect his wife is understandable, the method he's using—threatening to withdraw financial support—is morally unacceptable. It involves manipulation and coercion, which are unethical ways to influence someone's decision-making.
